title: Congratulations on the Promotion
author: jolein
summary: The piece uses the occasion of a teacher receiving a 'promotion' -- in this case, moving into an instructional coach role -- to examine how education confuses proximity to students with impact on students, and salary with worth. The author argues that the logic of educational career advancement pushes talented teachers away from direct student contact (where they have maximum impact) toward administrative and coaching roles (where their impact is diffuse and harder to measure) because the organizational reward structure treats moving away from the classroom as advancement. This creates a perverse incentive: the people best positioned to help the most students directly are systematically pulled toward roles where their student-contact hours drop to zero. The piece examines compensation, status, and recognition as the three reward mechanisms driving this pattern and argues for reimagining what 'promotion' could mean in education without requiring physical or relational distance from students.
points: * Educational career advancement pushes talented teachers away from direct student contact -- where their impact is highest -- toward coaching and administrative roles where their impact is diffuse and harder to measure. * The perverse incentive is structural: the people best positioned to help the most students directly are systematically rewarded for moving into roles with zero student-contact hours. * Three reward mechanisms drive the problem: compensation (higher pay typically requires leaving the classroom), status (coaching and administration are coded as 'more advanced'), and recognition (school culture celebrates promotions as achievements). * The piece distinguishes between impact (how many students are better off because of your work) and proximity (how close you are to students physically and relationally) -- education's career ladder conflates advancement with distance. * The author proposes that genuine promotion in education would mean more concentrated, higher-leverage student contact -- teaching more students, working with the hardest cases, mentoring novice teachers while remaining in the classroom.
quotes: We told her congratulations. We meant it. She is talented and the new role is real work. But somewhere in the congratulations there was a lie we didn't name: that moving away from students is progress. That spending less time with the people we said we got into this for is a reward.

The teacher who is best at teaching is the one we promote out of teaching. She becomes a coach. Her impact on students -- direct, daily, personal -- drops to near zero. Her impact on teachers -- diffuse, variable, hard to measure -- is supposed to compensate. Sometimes it does. Often it doesn't.

Salary is not worth. Salary is what the market has decided to pay you for what you do. In education, the market has decided to pay more for administration than for instruction. That tells you something about what the market values. It tells you nothing about what matters.

We could design it differently. We could decide that a 'master teacher' designation means you teach more students, work with the hardest cases, carry the heaviest instructional load -- and you get paid more for doing it, because harder work done better deserves more. We don't. We promote people out of the classroom and call it advancement.

The question I want to ask every teacher being congratulated on their promotion is this: are more students going to be better off because of what you're moving into? Not fewer students through more teachers -- more students, directly, personally, because of you. If the answer is no, we should ask ourselves what we're celebrating.
